items.question: How do you assess the relative importance of compute scaling and algorithmic innovation for improvements in AI performance?
items.object: The relative contributions of compute scaling and algorithmic innovation to AI performance
items.answer:
Scaling I think has been perhaps the central driver of the performance gains that we've seen in AI in the past decades on the depth and breadth of the capabilities that AI systems seem to be improving along. And so, you might look at key modern benchmarks like NMLU or GPT-3. And for those, it seems quite clear that maybe the majority of the variation in performance is explained just purely by the amount of compute used in training. We have done some research about trying to estimate this more rigorously. I co-authored a paper about the returns to compute scaling and the contributions from algorithmic innovations in language modeling. And there we find that about 2/3 of the variation in performance is due to scaling of pre-training compute. And this is performance in the language modeling task next to word prediction. For vision, we have done a similar work where again we find this equal match of the contributions, this roughly equal match of the contribution of scaling of training compute and non-scaling innovations, so this architecture and perhaps other things around data quality. And this is actually a fairly common picture in computer science more broadly.

So there are papers about the role of algorithmic innovations and compute scaling in domains like computer chess, like linear integer programs, SAT solvers, and the common picture there is that compute scaling is quite central to the performance improvements that we've seen in the past, you know, 30 years or more. And algorithmic innovations are also important and perhaps of equal importance to compute scaling. I think the algorithmic innovations in post-training recently have been quite impressive and perhaps that has surpassed, at least for some tasks, the contribution of compute scaling.

items.question: How do you put the fourfold annual growth in AI training compute into historical perspective?

That's been going on for over a decade now at this pace of about 4x per year. And this is really extraordinarily fast. So I looked at some other examples of these extremely fast scale-ups that we've seen in the history of technology. And even relative to those, it seems to be really in a class of its own. So the peak rate of adoption of mobile phones was about 2x per year for a period of 5 years or so. The peak rate of solar energy capacity installation was maybe about 50% per year. Really quite fast, but still not nearly as fast as a 4x per year for compute scaling. Then for the number of human genomes sequenced per year, I think this gets slightly closer to about 3x per year for a period of maybe 5 years or so. So, even relative to other extremely fast rates of technological capacity expansions, the scaling of compute seems just extraordinarily fast. And so I think this is really a defining trend of our current era that we're running through these orders of magnitude of compute extremely quickly and seeing this extraordinary expansion of the capabilities of these AI systems as a result.

items.question: How do you assess the feasibility of continuing to scale AI training compute at roughly four times per year through 2030?
items.object: The feasibility of continuing AI training compute scaling through 2030
items.answer: We find that it's quite likely that we can continue scaling up roughly at the rate that we've observed historically. So, at this 4x per year rate and we can probably continue doing this through the decade. And so what we do is we look at planned expansions from industry reports, from claims made by relevant companies, you know, TSMC for scaling the production of chips or data center companies and electricity providers for the scaling of power that is needed for training as well as estimates of the stock of data that's available to train these models. And for each of these, we look at them carefully and we conclude that yep, it probably permits this 10,000-fold scaling that is on trend for this decade. And this 10,000-fold scaling is roughly the difference in scale between GPT-2 and GPT-4. So, then we conclude that the similar jump that we've seen from GPT-2 and GPT-4 in terms of compute is something that is on trend with this 4x per year rate that we've seen the past 15 years, and it is also something that is quite plausible that we can continue to do and actually train models of that scale.

items.question: How do you expect scaling to change AI systems' ability to work independently by 2030?
items.object: Scaling AI toward greater agency and remote-worker capabilities by 2030
items.answer:
So, Jacob Steinhardt has this nice analogy where he compares these LLMs to interns or co-workers where there's some time scale at which you have to give feedback and engage with the outputs of the system. With current systems, every input-output, there you need to be involved. You need to steer it. You have to read the output and give it feedback and, you know, on the order of 1 minute you have to kind of hold its hand and tell it what to do. I think these systems as you scale them up become more coherent over longer horizons and they're able to perform longer-term actions and actually, you know, plan to do things that are useful. And so then it enables it to, you know, take these longer courses of actions where it requires fewer interventions from its users.

And so I think that might unlock some of this agency as well as making it more like a remote worker. Now, it's unclear whether in 2030, models that have been scaled up by maybe 10,000-fold will quite get to this kind of drop-in remote worker where, you know, you can basically give it some task and it's able to accomplish this very well. It's unclear, but I think that is something along that direction. And you know, something in that direction is perhaps its greater agency is something that might come out of this. The scaling as well as just better complex reasoning capabilities, more knowledge and understanding of even very obscure topics. And, you know, obscure branches of math and obscure, more niche applications or more niche fields of machine learning research. And a bunch of those things will probably appear as you scale these models up and as you provide them with more training data.

items.question: How do you understand diminishing returns to compute scaling in AI models?
items.object: Diminishing returns to compute scaling in AI models
items.answer: The usual way we think about these performance improvements as a function of just scaling them up is that this is log-linear. So, it's a straight line on a plot where you have log compute on the x-axis. And so, every doubling of compute gives you something like a linear improvement in some kind of performance metrics, like loss or accuracy or something like that. That is a common way of thinking about this. And so, that tells you that there are these diminishing returns, which is that you have to scale your compute exponentially to get linear gains in performance. Now, fortunately, compute is something that has been scaling exponentially. As we just talked about, this 4x per year growth rate. If this model of this log-linear performance with compute is correct, then you get this linear improvement over time. So, you know, I think this picture tells you that it becomes increasingly expensive to train models and to get this increment of performance improvement.

items.question: How do you see economies of scale creating increasing returns as AI systems become more capable and widely used?
items.object: Economies of scale and increasing returns in AI
items.answer:
For earlier systems like early language models like BERT or GPT-2, it just wasn't worth building a lot of really great tooling like what you have in ChatGPT with a code interpreter and what Claude has with artifacts and things like this because you just didn't have many users, and so spending that fixed cost didn't allow you to amortize this over a large number of users. And the same is true for the kind of cost that you incur during training. Just this one-time cost that you can amortize over the users that you have. And, you know, earlier on for these very small systems, it didn't make sense to spend all that much on those fixed costs because you couldn't amortize it over many users. You didn't have many users who were willing to pay for it. But now, you start to get more and more users as you improve the performance of these systems. And so this starts this flywheel where it starts to make sense to spend a lot more money on the training, on post-training, on building a really great way of interacting with these models, which before didn't quite make sense.

And then there's other reasons for increasing returns in AI that suggest that as we get more capable systems it makes sense to spend even more on making those useful. So one basic reason is, for instance, serving these models. There are economies of scale to serving as an API, and that's because your utilization of your hardware is better if you have large batches when you have many requests coming in with latency, then you can start to use your hardware much more efficiently.

If you just get one every second, then you have to run many H100s, many of these expensive data center GPUs, on just serving a single request. And that is just very expensive. But if you have millions, then you can start using your hardware more efficiently and that reduces these costs, and so you maybe are able to pass on these savings to your users. So from the user perspective it might seem like you get faster improvements because of these economies of scale.

items.question: How do you think AI systems will cross the threshold into becoming useful substitutes for humans?
items.object: The threshold at which autonomous AI systems become useful substitutes for humans
items.answer:

And this is, I think, an important barrier to getting these systems to become valuable. And so I do expect that once we get this degree of autonomy that's similar and agency that's similar to what humans typically might have, then you might get the flywheel where it actually starts to be useful and people start really spending a lot of money on improving this. I think one thing to recognize is that the human range itself is quite vast. I think this is something that the recent history of AI tells us, that sometimes it's easy to match median performance, but it's just really hard to match expert-level performance. And so I don't know if this is a threshold that you hit and then all of a sudden you're good. I think this is a bit more complicated because of this span of human range being potentially quite large.

And so I think there isn't this discontinuity, but there could be this acceleration as you start going through the human range where it starts to become more and more useful to actually substitute for humans, at least in some tasks in some cases.

items.question: How do you think uncertainty about AI's ability to automate human labor should affect investment in scaling AI?

items.question: How do you think investment in AI chips and supporting infrastructure should be timed relative to AI generating substantial economic value?
items.object: Investment in AI chips and supporting infrastructure ahead of economic returns
items.answer:
So, first of all, this friction around investors being uncertain and hesitant has been quite important. So, one particular case is with TSMC, which has been dragging its feet on expanding chip production because it's unsure whether AI will continue growing at the rate it has in the past. And so, without receiving advanced market commitments, where someone is promising to buy the output of new fabs, it's been somewhat reluctant to build out enough fabs to support the projected scaling. And there's some rumors where Sam Altman has asked for a bunch more production, and they've apparently been reluctant to get on board with that, and so there's this dragging of its feet that TSMC is doing. I think the more efficient allocation would probably involve a lot more spending and a lot more production of chips and related infrastructure right now. Like I expect that we will have these extremely large training runs and have a lot of compute that is going to be needed, and it is inefficient for that scaling to happen exactly when you need it.

You ideally want to scale this up beforehand because there are premiums that you otherwise have to pay where if you very suddenly want to expand your chip production then you have to pay this large premium on making that happen. The more efficient way of doing this would be to more smoothly ramp up production of chips and other capital stock like the energy infrastructure and the lithography machines and other things. So I think in order to avoid this large adjustment cost it makes more sense to do this initial expanded scaling even well in advance of when AI generates a lot of value. And that's because you want to avoid—it's not possible to perfectly time this. You have to prepare your supply chain ahead of time. An analogy for this is something like space colonization. In order to achieve very successful space colonization you might want to get really good at landing on the moon or something like that. Not because you care about landing on the moon but because it helps you flex those muscles.

And so I think that the more efficient thing we could be doing is in fact expand this computer-related capital stock and do these training runs to flex our muscles on being able to have the supply chain running as well as learn a lot about how to do this expansion, how to do these large training runs, and how to provide the energy and all the things that we need to support that.

items.question: Why do you think it makes economic sense to invest in AI compute infrastructure well before the expected returns arrive?

items.answer:

It takes on average maybe 2 years to build a fab and you can speed this up by spending more money on paying everyone a premium to get people to work longer, paying people to drop out of related jobs and join TSMC or ASML or OpenAI or whatever, or pay for these very large advanced market commitments and incur a bunch of risk this way. And this all comes with this premium, that it's harder to finance, that you have to pay for these types of adjustment costs. And this is inefficient because you could avoid this by spending things earlier. Investors shouldn't want to be caught out of the blue and suddenly realize that AI is going to be a big deal and suddenly have this frenzy of investment. Instead, the better thing would be for this investment to ramp up much more gradually. And that means that if you think that this investment will eventually happen, that you eventually will get trillion-dollar training runs or whatever, then it makes sense for quite a lot of the spending already to be happening.

And so, I think there is already this substantial updating that has happened. And I suspect more of this will happen in the future.

items.question: How do you assess the internet infrastructure build-out as an analogy for investment in AI?
items.object: The internet infrastructure build-out as an analogy for AI investment
items.answer:
I think the analogy of the internet is probably not a great analogy because AI just fundamentally seems like a much bigger deal because it promises this ability to flexibly substitute for human labor, which is this very important input into most economic production. And I think there's been very few of these technologies, like the computer, the internet, or what have you, where there is this good reason to expect that you get this kind of growth acceleration or something. And so, there isn't this very good reason that one would have had at the time to expect that the internet would have been an extremely large deal that I think we do have with AI today. So, I think the spending that we will do for AI eventually will far outstrip the spending that it would have made sense to do for the internet infrastructure there. So, for the internet, the fact that we did have this infrastructure investment that was front-loaded, that occurred before the internet generated this massive value, suggests that for AI, we might also have this investment that precedes when a lot of revenue is generated. And this, I think, will predictably result in people pointing out and being mystified by the fact that we're spending more than AI is currently generating, which is a common talking point among VCs.

And I think the response to that is that this investment is in large part made in the belief that AI in the future will generate this large payoff, not that current systems necessarily will generate a lot of value. And so, there might be this massive mismatch between this value generation and investment that we might see.

items.question: How do you understand the trade-off between inference compute and training compute in light of OpenAI's o1 model?
items.object: Scaling laws for inference compute
items.answer: Yeah, so there are scaling laws for inference compute and these have been around for some time. I think it's somewhat surprising that it has taken this long for OpenAI to implement something like this. So Andy Jones, who's a researcher at Anthropic, many years ago had this really nice paper where he showed these scaling laws for the game of Hex for scaling inference, and he showed that you can trade off inference and training compute. You can spend less training compute but more inference compute and get the same performance as a model with more training compute but less inference. And so you can have a larger model that is slower and more expensive to run being matched by a smaller model that is just run for longer, where maybe it does more reasoning or you sample from it more times and do some aggregation. So there are these scaling laws for inference, and you can do this kind of trade-off. So we had written about this in 2022 at Epoch and we made this prediction in our work where we said, you know, it seems possible that you can scale up inference and get the equivalent performance boost of one to two orders of magnitude of training compute with language models. items.question: What limits do you see to improving AI performance by giving a model more inference-time compute?
items.object: The limits of scaling inference-time compute
items.answer:
There was this funny Twitter poll that went viral, which asked if you had infinite time, would you be able to beat Gary Kasparov playing chess? A lot of people in AI tweeted about this, including Demis Hassabis. Demis said that the answer was no, that the average person just wouldn't be able to beat Gary Kasparov even with infinite time. You could think of having more time as scaling the inference budget that you give to a brain. And there's just no amount of scaling that gets you the same improvement in performance that something like better pre-training does. Having this brain that's just much better at doing this task that Gary Kasparov has for chess, there's no getting a worse brain for chess scaled up with inference compute to get it to perform at the same level.

I think the intuition here is quite right, though I disagree with the answer. There's a simple way of solving this, which is you just repeat the chess moves to Gary Kasparov each time. You play one move, you respond, you resign, and then you switch sides, and you play exactly Gary's response back. So you could solve this, but that's besides the point.

The point is that I think this intuition that there's a limit to the value of scaling inference compute is quite accurate. We do see this in examples for math, and someone at Scale AI had reproduced some of the inference scaling laws that OpenAI showed where there was this plateauing. There's some point at which it plateaus such that, even though it might be increasing, it's not going to get you all the way there. It's going to get really expensive and maybe not give you much in terms of improvement.

I think part of this is because for some of these tasks we don't have perfect verification. If you had some oracle that tells you whether the answer's correct, then you can just scale up the number of samples to extremely large numbers and you can continue getting some increments in performance. But without that I think it becomes a lot harder and you start to hit these diminishing returns.

We wrote something about this at Epoch, and we had done some estimates about the span of this trade-off. We summarized some evidence and then estimated that you could get maybe two orders of magnitude of equivalence in training compute. So you could scale up your inference by some large amount, and that gives you maybe at most two orders of magnitude of training-compute equivalent.

items.question: How do you think spending on AI inference compute should be balanced against spending on training compute?

items.question: How do you think AI compute spending should be allocated between training and inference?
items.object: Allocation of compute spending between AI training and inference
items.answer: I think the spending on inference compute is too little such that it makes sense to spend more on inference compute. There's a related blog post that we wrote recently where we made this point that the optimal amount of inference compute spending should be roughly half or roughly equivalent to the amount of training compute you're spending. It depends on precisely the class slope of the trade-off, but the basic intuition is that if you spend 99% of your budget on training compute and 1% on inference compute, you can double the amount of inference compute spending very cheaply and get a pretty substantial performance improvement. And so we made this point that you should expect inference and training compute spending to be on the same order because of this ability to trade these two things off against each other.

items.question: How do you think scaling up AI models affects the right balance between spending on inference compute and training compute?
items.object: The balance between inference and training compute as AI models scale
items.answer:
I think it makes sense to set your inference budget and your training budget something on par with each other. And so, you do get these returns to spending more inference, but you also get these returns to spending more training compute. I think the ratio between these two gets determined by this slope of this trade-off between inference and training compute. And there's a question of whether if you scale your model up, whether this slope changes, like whether the inference compute becomes relatively more valuable than training compute. And I think it's unclear. It might be the case that new techniques for doing inference appear and become feasible. So, there's this result that chain of thought is only useful at a particular scale. Like if you give GPT-2 chain of thought, it doesn't improve performance because it just loses track extremely quickly, and it just doesn't have the long-context reasoning ability to make use of this. Whereas GPT-4 certainly can make use of chain of thought and that increases performance. So, maybe you unlock these new techniques for using inference more efficiently that increase the returns to doing more inference and that might result in more inference spending.

But again, I think it doesn't make sense for these allocations to be imbalanced because when they are, then it starts to become very cheap to increase the one that is smaller. And you can often get performance improvements that way.

items.question: How do you assess whether Google and OpenAI are allocating compute efficiently between training and inference?

items.answer:
I think first of all, it's unclear exactly how they're spending their compute. We don't have enough data or information about exactly how many requests they're serving and how big these models are and how much it takes to serve these models and how much they're spending on training. First of all, this result that you should spend, if you want to optimally allocate compute, maybe very equal in both inference and training, is true on average, and it's fairly rough. But maybe 75/25 or something like that might also be optimal. Doesn't need to be exactly 50/50. It's also something that's true on average, over multiple years or averaged over a specific model generation.

The releases of models can be staggered, where first you have GPT-4o, and then months later you have GPT-4o Mini. And so, first you had to use this bulky, slow model for doing even very simple tasks. That's an inefficient use of your inference compute and ideally you want to do some kind of routing of the simple requests to smaller models. items.question: How do you understand the economic reasoning behind overtraining smaller AI models?

items.question: How do you assess whether algorithmic progress can support an accelerating feedback loop of automated AI research?
items.object: Algorithmic progress and the possibility of an accelerating automated R&D feedback loop
items.answer:
I think we've seen progress in terms of algorithmic improvements of broadly two types. So, one has been of the type of expanding the range of capabilities that models can do, and just making them better at pushing out the boundaries of what models can do. And the other type of algorithmic innovation has been reducing the cost of achieving already attained levels of capabilities. So, this would be things like distillation where you take a large model and distill it by generating synthetic data and training a smaller model to make that smaller model really quite capable and attain the existing capabilities. And so we've seen progress of both types, but maybe it's easier to achieve algorithmic progress that enables you to attain already attained levels of capabilities. And so it's a kind of make it easier to imitate GPT-4. And if it's the case that algorithmic innovations have mostly been making it possible to get the abilities of these larger models more cheaply, then having a lot of automated R&D might not actually expand the set of capabilities you can. And so there's one way in which it does, which is that if you make the model cheaper and smaller you can run more inference and then you can amplify your model and you can get some boost using this inference scaling.

But I think the argument that automating R&D results in this explosion of capabilities looks a lot weaker if algorithmic progress has been mostly of the sort that reduces the cost of achieving already attained capabilities. And then there's this other notion of algorithmic progress which just expands what you can do. And I think if that is something that we can automate doing, we can automate the R&D process that expands what these systems are able to do, then I think the argument that we get this feedback loop that results in accelerating progress looks slightly stronger. And so there's this question about what the nature of algorithmic progress really is. I think one reason to expect that algorithmic innovations have been a lot about reducing the costs of attaining existing capabilities is because if you look at something like Llama 3.1 it actually looks quite similar to GPT-2. It isn't that different, right? It's just much larger and so maybe expanding the frontier has been mostly about compute scaling and less about clever algorithmic tricks or something. I think that seems quite plausible.

At the same time you now have 8 billion or 1 billion parameter models that match the performance of 100 billion parameter models that we had years ago, like GPT-3 was, you know, 135 billion parameter models. We now have billion parameter models that get basically the same performance. And so, it seems like we're making a lot more progress on reducing costs, but not really expanding what we can do. Because Llama 3.1 looks pretty similar to GPT-2, and yet it's pretty close to GPT-4 and what labs are doing. And so, that suggests that maybe the algorithmic innovations that we're best at making is just reducing costs. And that is, I think, less likely to give rise to this kind of accelerating flywheel of automated R&D giving you better systems that are more capable, which enables you to make even more progress and get this kind of accelerating in capabilities.

items.question: How do you think the pace of expanding compute infrastructure will affect the timing of AI automation?

items.answer:

items.question: How do you think geographically distributing AI training could ease the power bottlenecks facing scaling through 2030?
items.object: Geographically distributed AI training as a way to ease power bottlenecks
items.answer:
One kind of interesting issue with energy or power is that for training, right now, the way that training usually happens is that a single campus or data center does the training run. And then you can serve this, you can infer the model across many different data centers. And so, the power demands for training are very highly concentrated. And this makes it run into these bottlenecks much more quickly, because there's only so much power you can get in Northern Virginia at a specific data center. And so that's why there's this struggle and companies are figuring out, can we get contracts with solar farms and nuclear power plants, and there's plans for reopening Three Mile Island for powering data centers.

One thing you can do is you can geographically distribute your training. You can involve a data center in Northern Virginia, a data center in Pennsylvania, and in many other places. And then you can effectively distribute the power that you need in order to train a model and tap into more energy sources. In this report about can we scale through 2030, we worked out that yes, indeed you can do this geographic distribution of your training run.

Now, it requires running a lot of fiber optic cables, but that's something AT&T and other people do, and we have fiber optic cable across oceans. And so, running fiber optic cables is certainly something that it's feasible to do. And that already gets you more breathing room and enables you to tap into more energy infrastructure. And so, even without building a lot of energy infrastructure, I suspect that you can already do quite a bit of scaling. A model that's 10,000 times greater than GPT-4 that is on trend for 2030, that's about 5 GW or something. In the US, the total installed capacity is about 1,000 GW. This is 0.5%. Quite a lot, but in some sense if it's the most important industrial technology or whatever, then I think this seems well justified.

items.question: How do you think society would respond to AI systems broadly able to substitute for human labor?
items.object: Society’s response to AI systems broadly able to substitute for human labor
items.answer:
Well, one thing to say is that I'm really quite uncertain about both the question of whether in the next five or 10 years we will get such systems that are broadly able to substitute for humans. I think I have a fair amount of uncertainty about that. So, I don't think this is something that's assured to happen. I'm also quite uncertain about what the precise response, if this were to happen, what exactly the effects on society would be. I have some guesses about what happens to wages. I think there will be in some cases much higher wages, and then there will be a lot of displacement. I think there are costs associated with this transition and labor displacement. There's also a lot of value that's generated. Like AI just has this ability to boost our wealth and technology, and that is extremely valuable. And I suspect people will, if and when we get much more capable AI systems that generate a lot of economic value, get really excited about some of this. You know, the medical innovations that you might get are really quite tremendous. And so there will be a lot of pressure to adopt and build some of these technologies.

You know, I also think that people will be quite concerned about this displacement of human labor, which potentially creates unemployment. That's not always the case. You can find jobs elsewhere and new tasks are generated. And so there's going to be a lot of upheaval and movement, and people will have a lot of concerns about this. There's also this concern around disempowerment of humans and humans having less control and oversight and things like this. And I think some of those concerns are also valid, and I suspect that there will be this societal response that is driven by some of these concerns around empowerment, control, oversight. I think it's worth thinking a lot more about precisely how this is going to be handled, which is precisely why I'm working on this and why we founded Epoch to improve and inform these discussions and the kind of policy that ends up responding to what's happening in AI, what will continue happening, and the effects that this will have.

items.question: How do you use past AI capability advances and compute scaling to assess how far we are from automating remote work?
items.object: Compute scaling and the remaining capabilities needed to automate remote work
items.answer: I think what Ege is referring to is, if you look at the past 10 years of AI progress, we've gone through about nine or 10 orders of magnitude of compute, and we got various capabilities that were unlocked. So in the early period, people were solving gameplay on specific games, on very complex games. And that happened from 2015 to 2020, Go and Chess and Dota and other games. And then you had maybe sophisticated language capabilities that were unlocked with these large language models, and maybe advanced abstract reasoning and coding and maybe math. That was maybe another big capability that got unlocked. And so maybe there are a couple of these big unlocks that happened over the past 10 years, but that happened on the order of once every three years or so, or maybe one every three orders of magnitude of compute scaling. And then you might ask the question, “How many more such competencies might we need to unlock in order to be able to have an AI system that can match the capabilities of humans across the board?” Maybe specifically just on remote work tasks. And so then you might ask, well, maybe you need kind of coherence over very long horizons, or you need agency and autonomy, or maybe you need full multimodal understanding, just like a human would. And then you ask the question, “Okay, how long might that take?” And so you can think about, well, just in terms of calendar years, the previous unlocks took about—you get one every three years or so. But of course, that previous period coincided with this rapid scale-up of the amount of compute that we use for training. So we went through maybe 9 or 10 orders of magnitude since AlexNet compared to the biggest models we have today. And we're getting to a level where it's becoming harder and harder to scale up compute. And we've done some extrapolations and some analysis looking at specific constraints, like energy or GPU production. And based on that, it looks like we might have maybe three or four orders of magnitude of scaling left. And then you're really spending a pretty sizable fraction or a non-trivial fraction of world output on just building up data centers, energy infrastructure, fabs, and so on.

items.question: What convinced you that Ege Erdil should work on economic questions at Epoch?
items.object: Ege Erdil’s knowledge of economics and suitability for Epoch
items.answer: We connected on a Discord for Metaculus, which is this forecasting platform. And I was a graduate student at Cambridge at the time doing research in economics. And I was having conversations with my peers there. And I was occasionally having conversations with Ege. And I was like, “This guy knows a lot more about economics”. And at the time he was a computer science undergrad in Ankara. And he knows more about economics and about these big trends in economic growth and economic history than almost any of my peers at the university. And so, like, what the hell is up with that? And then we started having frequent collaborations and ended up hiring Ege for Epoch because it clearly makes sense for him to work on these types of questions.

items.question: Why did you see starting Epoch as a better way to pursue the research you were excited about?
items.object: The decision to start Epoch
items.answer: So I was at MIT doing more research, and I was pretty unhappy with the bureaucracy there where it was very hard for me to scale projects up, hire people. And I was pretty excited about a bunch of work that my PI wasn't excited about because it's maybe hard to publish or it doesn't confer the same prestige. And so I was chatting with Jaime Sevilla, one of the co-founders, and we just collaborated on projects and then thought we should just start our own org, because we can just hire people and work on the projects we were excited about.

items.question: What opportunity did you see in founding Epoch to study the future of AI?
items.object: The motivation for founding Epoch
items.answer: It was more like we can make a bunch of progress because clearly academia and industry is kind of dropping the ball on a bunch of important questions that academia is unable to publish interesting papers on. Industry is not really focused on producing useful insights. And so it seemed very good for us to just do that. And also the timing was very good. So we started just before ChatGPT and we wanted to have much more grounded discussions of the future of AI. And I was frustrated with the quality of discussion that was happening on the internet about the future of AI. And to some extent or to a very large extent, I still am. And that's a large part of what motivates me to do this. It's just born out of frustration with bad thinking and arguments about where AI is going to go.
